title: Jamie Goode: Old vines won’t survive on sentiment alone
summary:

The post Jamie Goode: Old vines won’t survive on sentiment alone appeared first on winemag.
content:
Wine has been going through some changes. It has always been going through changes, to be honest. In classic wine-producing regions, we’ve had a long shift from the need for large quantities of cheap wine to feed the heroic thirst of the masses. People in Portugal, France, Italy and Spain used to drink a lot of wine. The big need was for volume, and so industries geared to supply lots of cheap wine have been retrofitted to produce better quality wine for a more discerning and less thirsty customer base. It has been an uncomfortable process, and it’s still ongoing. In other countries wine has been growing and people have been drinking more, but even this growth has seen a bit of contraction of late. And it’s uncomfortable to watch, because people and their livelihoods are impacted.

The danger is that in this contraction process, it’s not only the less impressive vineyards that are being pulled out, but also some rather special vineyards. A case in point is in the notorious vine pull in Australia in the 1980s, where some very special old vineyards in regions such as the Barossa were taken out. Because of the absence of phylloxera in South Australia, the Barossa has a lot of old, ungrafted vines. There are more than 100 hectares of centenarian vineyards there.

And in Spain, were it not for the efforts of Comando G and their buddies, many of the amazing old Garnacha vineyards that simply weren’t profitable would have been pulled out. It’s strange how fashion changes: in the peak Parker era everyone wanted big, dark, bold wines – something that Garnacha can’t do easily. Now we cherish the fragrant, lighter-coloured reds that old vine Garnacha is an absolute specialist at.

Globally, there are many special old vineyards. They are a treasure, but they aren’t always treasured. Should there be laws protecting them?

When I was at university, one of the courses I took in my degree in biological science was on conservation and wildlife management. I really enjoyed it, to the point that I even considered doing a research job in ecology. There were two things I took away from this course. One is that if you want to conserve rare species, you need to focus on preserving their habitat. The second was that the only conservation that really works is conservation that pays. If an ecosystem or a species becomes an economic resource, then people will preserve them.

This is exactly the approach that has been taken by the Old Vine Project in South Africa, and it has been fantastic to watch this amazing initiative develop. And I guess imitation is the sincerest form of flattery: the model has been adopted by others. When Rosa Kruger set out to produce a list of vineyards over 35 years old in South Africa, this gave producers in search of old vines a chance to connect with growers. Previously, the fruit from many of these vineyards was being sold too cheaply, and disappearing into big blends where its origin was never recognized.

How do you keep precious old vineyards in the ground, rather than let them be bulldozed? I guess you could give them protected status, but for a vineyard to continue, it has to be farmed, and you can’t force a farmer to maintain a vineyard if they aren’t making money for it. And governments can’t easily pay farmers to preserve some vineyards and not others.

The best way to keep great vines in the ground is to value them. And the Old Vine Project does just this. Winemakers with ambition buy grapes from heritage vineyards and pay a premium that makes farming them pay. The growers are rewarded, and the bulldozers stay away. The Old Vine heritage seal is a great initiative here, and it means that suddenly cooperatives who were previously putting old vine grapes into an inexpensive wine can now make a separate wine from the old vines, add the heritage sticker, and charge R200 for the bottle. The seal acts as a strong buying cue. Everyone benefits.

Part of the dynamic here is having ambitious landless winemakers who want to make something special, and are able to because there is a culture of growers owning vineyards who are willing to sell these grapes. South Africa has a nice dynamic where winemakers working for large companies are allowed to do a bit of home brew: to start their own brand. Sometimes there are restrictions: perhaps a case limit of the new brand, or a stipulation that they use varieties other than used by their employer, to avoid conflict of interest situations. But the general permissiveness of winery owners in allowing their winemakers to have side projects is good for everyone, I think. It keeps the winemaker fulfilled professionally, it allows them to build their own brand gradually, and the dynamism created by new producers and new projects is good for the overall health of South African wine.

And, of course, this creates customers for old heritage vineyards, keeping them in the ground.

On a regional level, there is something to be said for legislation to protect significant vineyards. This is important where land has value for redevelopment. If it is zoned so that no one can build homes, but it has to be kept as agricultural land, then this is valuable. Urban spread is threatening many wine regions, and some legislation could help here. I was recently in the Hunter Valley, a brilliant historically significant Australian wine region. With its proximity to Sydney, this is quite a playground for city folk. If economics is left to decide the destiny of the land, then it’s likely that the vineyard area will further contract. You could end up with a wine region popular with tourists, but with hardly any vineyards.

But the best way to preserve important vineyards? Make them pay!

  • Jamie Goode is a London-based wine writer, lecturer, wine judge and book author. With a PhD in plant biology, he worked as a science editor, before starting wineanorak.com, one of the world’s most popular wine websites.

title: Editorial: Wine needs new consumers. Now what?
summary:
Over the weekend, a group of perhaps a dozen adults gathered around a braai. Two-thirds were English-speaking, one-third Afrikaans-speaking – an unusual enough combination to prompt a conversation about language. Why, someone asked, was I not fluent in Afrikaans despite having studied at Stellenbosch University? My response was that, at least, I had Afrikaans friends. […]

The post Editorial: Wine needs new consumers. Now what? appeared first on winemag.
content:
Over the weekend, a group of perhaps a dozen adults gathered around a braai. Two-thirds were English-speaking, one-third Afrikaans-speaking – an unusual enough combination to prompt a conversation about language. Why, someone asked, was I not fluent in Afrikaans despite having studied at Stellenbosch University? My response was that, at least, I had Afrikaans friends. What struck me afterwards was that I couldn’t say the same about having black friends.

The global wine industry faces a challenge that is now impossible to look past: consumers are drinking less.

There is less agreement about why. Demographic change, health concerns, economic pressure and competition from other alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages are all offered as explanations. The causes matter, but perhaps less than the consequence. Wine has a demand problem, and the old growth models are no longer available to solve it.

That ought to prompt a more radical question than how we tell wine’s story: What if the industry needs to change the way wine is experienced, discovered and discussed?

It dawned on me that a key part of the problem is not poor communication of a compelling consumer promise, but a lack of relevance at a more fundamental level. I wrote about this earlier this year, arguing that wine’s problem isn’t a shortage of stories but a shortage of reasons for people to care. That remains my view. The harder question is what needs to change.

Technology: opportunity or trivialisation?

The danger is that technology makes wine more accessible while making it more trivial. Wine has enthusiastically embraced digital marketing while remaining remarkably attached to analogue ways of helping people choose what to drink.

A consumer still encounters a shelf containing dozens of bottles, differentiated by labels, regions, varieties, vintages and producer names. The information required to make a confident choice can be considerable.

Technology can make this easier. AI, for example, could become a useful wine intermediary – not a robot sommelier making grandiose pronouncements, but a tool that translates expertise into the questions ordinary drinkers actually ask.

Is this dry? Full-bodied? Fresh and linear or soft and smooth-textured? What should I eat with it? Is there something similar but cheaper? If I liked this bottle, what else might I enjoy? Is this a wine to drink tonight or keep for five years?

These are not intellectually inferior questions. They are the questions that get wine into people’s glasses.

The opportunity, then, is not to use technology to produce more wine content. There is already plenty of that. It is to reduce the effort required to participate in wine. We don’t need an infinite number of tasting notes generated by machines – God forbid, humans are already adequate at that. We need better ways of connecting a particular person with a particular wine.

But there is a caution. Personalisation can easily become another form of narrowing, giving us more of what we already like while reducing the chance of encountering something unexpected. At the same time, digital wine culture has its own cliques, and the people within them can end up deciding what is fashionable, desirable or worth talking about. Technology may therefore democratise access to wine while creating new forms of gatekeeping around taste.

Its more interesting role would be to do the opposite: broaden discovery, expose people to wines and ideas beyond the circles they already inhabit, and make it easier for new voices to influence what wine becomes.

Who gets to define wine?

I am 55, white, male and based in Cape Town. I have spent more than two decades working professionally in wine. I know a great deal about the subject and have accumulated plenty of assumptions about what matters in wine, how it should be discussed and what constitutes expertise.

But the episode around the braai left me wondering how well equipped I am to understand what might make wine relevant to people whose lives and experiences have historically had so little meaningful contact with it. If my own social world can remain so racially circumscribed after 55 years in South Africa, perhaps the wine industry should be less surprised that its attempts to connect with black consumers so often feel superficial.

My experience has value. But it does not make me the ideal interlocutor with every future wine consumer. This is particularly pertinent when we talk about South Africa’s emerging Black middle class. The answer isn’t simply to market wine more effectively to Black consumers. Nor is it to recruit a handful of Black personalities as ambassadors while leaving the underlying culture untouched.

If new consumers are to become part of wine’s future, they need a genuine role in shaping it. That means more Black winemakers, yes, but also more Black retailers, sommeliers, marketers, educators, writers and entrepreneurs with the power to influence the category. It means allowing different social occasions, tastes and cultural references to shape how wine is presented and consumed.

And it means those of us who have traditionally occupied positions of authority accepting that relevance may involve giving up some control over the conversation. That isn’t a threat to expertise. It is a test of whether expertise can adapt.

The wine industry sometimes treats the new consumer as though they are waiting to be persuaded to appreciate what we already appreciate. That is the wrong starting point.

The more productive question is: what might wine become when people who have historically been outside its cultural centre start influencing it?

The answer should not be “wine dumbed down”. Nor should it be “wine as we know it, but with younger faces”. Nor should it be wine reinvented so completely that it loses any connection with its history.

The industry should retain the things that make wine worth caring about – place, craft, history, agriculture, diversity and pleasure – while becoming much less prescriptive about how consumers encounter them.

That may mean different formats, occasions, price points, voices and ways of talking about taste. It may mean wine appearing in spaces where it has not traditionally appeared, alongside food, music and culture without demanding that everyone first learn its vocabulary. One of the reasons I detest “minerality” as a descriptor is that it illustrates the problem perfectly: what insiders regard as useful shorthand can sound like nonsense to everyone else.

And it may mean accepting that some of the things enthusiasts consider important simply aren’t important to everyone else. That is not necessarily decline. It may be democratisation.

As we know all too well, vineyards are being pulled out and production is contracting. The difficult work now is not managing abundance but rebuilding demand. We cannot assume that the next generation will inherit wine culture simply because previous generations did. They have more choices, different media habits and different relationships with authority. They also have no obligation to preserve our hierarchies.

So what would I suggest? Use technology to make wine easier to discover and understand, without reducing it to disposable content. Communicate in ways that begin with consumers’ lives rather than wine’s internal vocabulary. Create more opportunities for participation rather than simply more opportunities to consume marketing. And, above all, broaden who gets to shape the category.

For someone like me, there is a final responsibility: to remain useful without assuming that I must remain central. That may be the hardest adjustment of all.

title: Recipe: Tofu, tat soi and shimeji mushroom stir-fry
summary:
Delicious served with steamed rice. Serves 4 Ingredients: 3 tbsp (45ml) sunflower oil 400g tofu, drained and patted dry with absorbent paper 60g shimeji mushrooms, cleaned ¼ cup (60ml) ginger, finely chopped 2 tsp (10ml) sesame seed oil 3 tbsp (45ml) soy sauce 3 tbsp (45ml) sweet chilli sauce squeeze of lemon 200g tat soi, […]

The post Recipe: Tofu, tat soi and shimeji mushroom stir-fry appeared first on winemag.
content:
Serve with Kruger Family Wines Old Vines Cinsault 2017.

Delicious served with steamed rice.

Serves 4

Ingredients:
3 tbsp (45ml) sunflower oil
400g tofu, drained and patted dry with absorbent paper
60g shimeji mushrooms, cleaned
¼ cup (60ml) ginger, finely chopped
2 tsp (10ml) sesame seed oil
3 tbsp (45ml) soy sauce
3 tbsp (45ml) sweet chilli sauce
squeeze of lemon
200g tat soi, washed
15g coriander, chopped
steamed basmati rice, to serve

Method:
Cube tofu into bite size portions and set aside.

Heat sunflower oil in a non-stick pan until hot and gently shallow-fry tofu until golden brown and crispy. Add mushrooms and ginger and stir-fry for further five  minutes. Add sesame oil, soy sauce, sweet chilli sauce and a squeeze of lemon.

Toss in tat soi and remove pan from heat allowing the leaves to wilt. Check seasoning.

Serve with steamed basmati rice and fresh coriander.

Wine pairing:
Light-bodied reds you can chill will work with this dish – think Pinot Noir or new-wave Cinsault.

  • Recipe supplied by Source Food – a Cape Town-based food agency that specializes in experiential marketing. They will create a recipe or meal to communicate your brand’s message.

title: Tim James: Growing older, drinking differently
summary:
We know about old vines and old wines – and their age makes a difference. But what about old wine-drinkers? Does age bring changes, for better or worse, in taste-experiences and preferences? It was a question that the American winewriter and -importer Terry Theise raised in the latest issue of World of Fine Wine, prompted […]

The post Tim James: Growing older, drinking differently appeared first on winemag.
content:
We know about old vines and old wines – and their age makes a difference. But what about old wine-drinkers? Does age bring changes, for better or worse, in taste-experiences and preferences? It was a question that the American winewriter and -importer Terry Theise raised in the latest issue of World of Fine Wine, prompted by his own experience (he didn’t announce it there, but tells me he’s 73). This led to wondering about physical changes that might prompt changes in taste: a supposed reduction in acuity, for example; and he mentioned the presumably hormonal changes in older women – but I guess those in men might also be expected to have consequences.

Theise was surprised, however, to find that most of the small handful of wine-professional friends and colleagues he consulted reported no significant patterns of change in their wine-tastes.

I too am surprised. Easy continuity is not my own experience, whatever the causes of my shifts. Given that I’ve noticeably changed my tastes in various aesthetic areas that are important to me, why not my wine-drinking? These days I seldom read novels, for example, and novel-reading was a defining factor of my life for decades, professional and personal. Overall I now read less than I used to, and it’s usually re-reading rather than anything new, and more often than not it’s non-fiction. My musical tastes have shifted too: it’s still all “classical”, but I can’t easily recall how much I used to love Italian opera (mostly unspeakably silly stuff, I now think, though often kitschly beautiful); and generally I have moved in both temporal directions away from the lushness of nineteenth-century Romanticism.

So, again, why not changes in my tastes in wine as I’ve got older? I’m now 71, having begun a more-or-less serious relationship with wine only in my latter 30s. I don’t think these changes are all obviously ascribable to bodily changes any more than are my shifts in musical and literary tastes … but, yes, maybe some. I have certainly had a general reduction in my taste for sweet foods and drinks in the last decade or two, and that is plausibly related to bodily changes. So my beloved older-style German rieslings often seem too sweet and I would reluctantly admit to, on the whole, preferring drier ones.

When acidity loses its appeal

This is something that Terry Theise strongly notices too. Interestingly (given the high acidity in the best of those sweet rieslings) he also notes a change that he says is more age-typical: a resistance to very high acidity in wines, a character he used to relish. I hadn’t thought of that for myself, but I think it applies. It would help explain why at tastings I seem to object more than my younger colleagues to the “hipster” style of lowish-alcohol, ultra-fresh wines, both white and red, and tend to find them unbalanced and even aggressive in their acidity.

Taking this further, I wonder if this also accounts for my mild turn in the last decade or so away from the red burgundies and local pinot noirs that I previously enjoyed so much more. I’ve returned more , in fact, to an earlier love: cabernet sauvignon-based blends – especially from Bordeaux, especially the dark-fruited, savoury, tannic and “sinister” ones that hark back to pre-1982 times (but seldom South African examples, which I can admire theoretically occasionally, but seldom love, because they are that bit too sunny and friendly, even when not too ripe and powerful). Tannin, then, suits me now more than acidity, it seems.

The pleasures of caring less

As to a decline in acuity – well, I don’t think I’ve ever been acute as a taster, nor have I aspired to become more so, though I realise that this might seem odd for someone who, for example, tasted and rated for the annual Platter’s Guide for two decades. Aiming for the finest, geekiest discrimination has never interested me nearly as much as other aspects of wine (social, historical, cultural, agricultural) – even less now. Decades back, I got through giving up smoking cigarettes without being aware that it made much difference to my palate. Having now joyfully abandoned writing more than the briefest of tasting notes has been an enormous liberation. (I can’t say I frequently read others’ notes either.) It’s very possible that this liberation has itself positively affected the way I enjoy wine in all circumstances: an aura of anxiousness – coming from a sense of responsibility and of my likely inadequacy – doesn’t cloud the pleasure.

There’s much less detail that I’m concerned with these days, Possibly that marks a decline. But I read, just this morning over my toast and marmalade, this apposite line from Montaigne about the comfort he finds in old age, in an essay entitled “All things have their season”:  “that it deadens in me many desires and cares by which life is troubled”, including “care for knowledge”. There’s so much about the vast world of wine that I no longer feel curious about, as I did when I would read the Oxford Companion to Wine cover to cover. That reduction in interest is more of an admission, I suppose, than a boast.

Some changes in my tastes – as reflected in my drinking practices – are clearly not so much so much about ageing as about my growing older in a particular place and time. I’ve had a good few decades chronicling – and drinking – the Cape wine revolution. South African fine white wine is, widely, a miraculously delicate, not to mention delicious, expression of its origins. In response, I now drink nearly as much white wine as red, and that’s a notable shift. As all wine gets more expensive, local and foreign, and I don’t get richer, it suits me well to buy and drink for my pleasure lots of Cape white, and little foreign white apart from sherry and what good German riesling I can afford.

As for the local reds, I prefer the Rhône-style ones, based on syrah or grenache – the whole range of them, including the lighter, fresher ones (but not too light) with no new oak. There’s another change, I think: I now get more pleasure than before from comparatively simple, fairly young wines. I don’t think I’d even want to drink only fine, mature, serious wines, even as an aspiration. Perhaps it’s a sign of greater tolerance.

Something else. I’ve always had a particular passion for fortified wine: sherry, port, madeira. But now, along with drinking some younger, lighter wines, I also go to the opposite extreme and drink a good amount of brandy. I seem to like that kick at the end of the day. My total alcohol consumption has probably declined a little in the last decade, but the proportion of the alcohol intake provided by brandy has increased.

That’s a change in my drinking habits that I am at a total loss to explain. The great revolutionary Leon Trotsky once said that “’Old age is the most unexpected of all things that can happen to a man.” That’s true, I think, and many of the details of the process are just as surprising.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.

title: Aspiring Top Drop Awards 2026: 22 wines delivering exceptional value
summary:

The post Aspiring Top Drop Awards 2026: 22 wines delivering exceptional value appeared first on winemag.
content:
We tasted 92 wines retailing for R120 or less. Twenty-two scored 91 points or higher, qualifying them to carry the Top Drop sticker.

From these, we’ve selected 10 standout buys – wines that combine particularly high quality with an especially attractive price. The remaining 12 also qualify as Top Drops and are listed below.

Top 10 Best Buys

Ranked by quality, with price considered in assessing overall value.

1. Nederburg Baronne 2024

44% Cabernet Sauvignon, 42% Shiraz, the rest Petit Verdot, Tannat, Durif, Malbec and Carignan. Engaging aromatics of red and black berries, fynbos, flowers and a hint of pepper. Light-bodied with fresh acidity and a gently savoury finish. Not massively intense in terms of weight or flavour, but by no means simple – unshowy and highly likeable.

Score:

93

Price:

R100

2. Wild House Chardonnay 2025 (Wildeberg)

Top notes of flowers and herbs before lemon, peach and the merest hint of vanilla on the nose while the palate is rich and textured but equally vital thanks to vibrant acidity. Well balanced and rather seductive.

Score:

93

Price:

R110

3. De Wet Chenin Blanc 2026

Very primary and inviting aromatics of guava, citrus and peach plus hints of flowers and herbs. The palate is clean and fresh with good fruit concentration, crisp acidity and a dry finish. Well balanced and entirely unassuming.

Score:

92

Price:

R69

4. Riebeek Cellars Collection Shiraz 2025

Just a little flinty reduction gives way to red berries, fynbos, rose and white pepper on the nose. The palate is light-bodied with juicy fruit, fresh acidity and fine tannins, with a faint savoury quality to the finish. Modest in scale but full of appeal.

Score:

92

Price: 

R88

5. Leyland Chenin Blanc 2026 (De Wet)

Aromatics of herbs, lime, lemon, a hint of guava and touch of leesy complexity. The palate has good weight and texture, with moderate acidity providing balance and a gently savoury finish bringing it to a neat close.

Score:

92

Price: 

R90

6. Durbanville Hills Cabernet Sauvignon 2024

Red and black berries, some leafiness, with a pleasant hint of smokiness on the nose. The palate is clean and fresh with fine tannins, the finish dry. True to the variety, unimposing, honest.

Score:

92

Price: 

R100

7. Koelenbosch Shiraz 2023 (Koelenhof)

The nose shows red and black berries, a touch of violets and black pepper. The palate is luscious and juicy with moderate acidity and a gently savoury finish.

Score:

92

Price: 

R105

8. Bellingham Homestead Sauvignon Blanc 2025

Herbal notes lead into bell pepper, grapefruit, granadilla and pineapple on the nose. The palate is rich and rounded, with well-integrated, tangy acidity and a gently savoury finish. At this price, it’s difficult to ask for much more.

Score:

92

Price: 

R115

9. Zorgvliet Silver Myn Argentum 2024

56% Merlot, 27% Cabernet Franc, 14% Cabernet Sauvignon, 3% Petit Verdot. Red and black berries, violets, a leafy note, earth and meat stock on the nose. Medium bodied with juicy fruit, good freshness and fine tannins. Lively with a nicely savoury finish. Classic in style, unshowy in execution.

Score:

92

Price: 

R118

10. Salt Rock Chenin Blanc 2025

Attractive aromatics of honeysuckle, herbs, citrus and green apple. The palate has concentrated fruit yet comes across as taut and austere in structure, with punchy acidity and a particularly dry finish. Elegant and nuanced.

Score:

92

Price: 

R120

Also Top Drop

These 12 wines also scored 91 points or higher and retail for R120 or less.

What is a Top Drop?

Top Drop is Winemag’s shortlist of wines that combine high quality with affordability. To qualify, a wine had to retail for R120 or less and score at least 91 points in our tasting.

Look for the Top Drop sticker in stores.

Winner benefits

Each category winner received R5,000 in shipping from Aspiring Couriers.

title: Burgundy dominates the world’s most expensive wines
summary:
Burgundy’s dominance at the top end of the fine-wine market is extraordinary. Investment platform WineCap’s 2026 ranking of the 25 most expensive wines contains 24 Burgundies, with only Domaine Jean-Louis Chave’s Ermitage Cathelin from the northern Rhône breaking the region’s hold. Even more striking, 17 wines come from Domaine Leroy and Domaine d’Auvenay, both owned […]

The post Burgundy dominates the world’s most expensive wines appeared first on winemag.
content:
Burgundy’s dominance at the top end of the fine-wine market is extraordinary. Investment platform WineCap’s 2026 ranking of the 25 most expensive wines contains 24 Burgundies, with only Domaine Jean-Louis Chave’s Ermitage Cathelin from the northern Rhône breaking the region’s hold.

Even more striking, 17 wines come from Domaine Leroy and Domaine d’Auvenay, both owned by Lalou Bize-Leroy, together accounting for 64.1% of the ranking’s combined value.

At the top is Domaine de la Romanée-Conti’s Romanée-Conti Grand Cru at £195,406 per 12-bottle case (roughly equivalent to R352,000 a bottle at today’s exchange rate), followed by Domaine d’Auvenay’s Chevalier-Montrachet Grand Cru at £186,419 per case (R336,000 a bottle).

For perspective, Pétrus, Bordeaux’s highest-ranked wine, sits only 46th in the wider ranking, while Krug Clos du Mesnil, Champagne’s highest entry, is 80th.

The lesson is fairly simple. At the very top of the wine market, scarcity, provenance and reputation can count for more than points. Burgundy happens to possess extraordinary quantities of all three – but the remarkable concentration of value around Lalou Bize-Leroy suggests that, at this level, the market is pricing not just wine but access to something that cannot readily be reproduced.

title: Jamie Goode: Old vines won’t survive on sentiment alone
summary:
Wine has been going through some changes. It has always been going through changes, to be honest. In classic wine-producing regions, we’ve had a long shift from the need for large quantities of cheap wine to feed the heroic thirst of the masses. People in Portugal, France, Italy and Spain used to drink a lot […]

The post Jamie Goode: Old vines won’t survive on sentiment alone appeared first on winemag.
content:
Wine has been going through some changes. It has always been going through changes, to be honest. In classic wine-producing regions, we’ve had a long shift from the need for large quantities of cheap wine to feed the heroic thirst of the masses. People in Portugal, France, Italy and Spain used to drink a lot of wine. The big need was for volume, and so industries geared to supply lots of cheap wine have been retrofitted to produce better quality wine for a more discerning and less thirsty customer base. It has been an uncomfortable process, and it’s still ongoing. In other countries wine has been growing and people have been drinking more, but even this growth has seen a bit of contraction of late. And it’s uncomfortable to watch, because people and their livelihoods are impacted.

The danger is that in this contraction process, it’s not only the less impressive vineyards that are being pulled out, but also some rather special vineyards. A case in point is in the notorious vine pull in Australia in the 1980s, where some very special old vineyards in regions such as the Barossa were taken out. Because of the absence of phylloxera in South Australia, the Barossa has a lot of old, ungrafted vines. There are more than 100 hectares of centenarian vineyards there.

And in Spain, were it not for the efforts of Comando G and their buddies, many of the amazing old Garnacha vineyards that simply weren’t profitable would have been pulled out. It’s strange how fashion changes: in the peak Parker era everyone wanted big, dark, bold wines – something that Garnacha can’t do easily. Now we cherish the fragrant, lighter-coloured reds that old vine Garnacha is an absolute specialist at.

Globally, there are many special old vineyards. They are a treasure, but they aren’t always treasured. Should there be laws protecting them?

When I was at university, one of the courses I took in my degree in biological science was on conservation and wildlife management. I really enjoyed it, to the point that I even considered doing a research job in ecology. There were two things I took away from this course. One is that if you want to conserve rare species, you need to focus on preserving their habitat. The second was that the only conservation that really works is conservation that pays. If an ecosystem or a species becomes an economic resource, then people will preserve them.

This is exactly the approach that has been taken by the Old Vine Project in South Africa, and it has been fantastic to watch this amazing initiative develop. And I guess imitation is the sincerest form of flattery: the model has been adopted by others. When Rosa Kruger set out to produce a list of vineyards over 35 years old in South Africa, this gave producers in search of old vines a chance to connect with growers. Previously, the fruit from many of these vineyards was being sold too cheaply, and disappearing into big blends where its origin was never recognized.

How do you keep precious old vineyards in the ground, rather than let them be bulldozed? I guess you could give them protected status, but for a vineyard to continue, it has to be farmed, and you can’t force a farmer to maintain a vineyard if they aren’t making money for it. And governments can’t easily pay farmers to preserve some vineyards and not others.

The best way to keep great vines in the ground is to value them. And the Old Vine Project does just this. Winemakers with ambition buy grapes from heritage vineyards and pay a premium that makes farming them pay. The growers are rewarded, and the bulldozers stay away. The Old Vine heritage seal is a great initiative here, and it means that suddenly cooperatives who were previously putting old vine grapes into an inexpensive wine can now make a separate wine from the old vines, add the heritage sticker, and charge R200 for the bottle. The seal acts as a strong buying cue. Everyone benefits.

Part of the dynamic here is having ambitious landless winemakers who want to make something special, and are able to because there is a culture of growers owning vineyards who are willing to sell these grapes. South Africa has a nice dynamic where winemakers working for large companies are allowed to do a bit of home brew: to start their own brand. Sometimes there are restrictions: perhaps a case limit of the new brand, or a stipulation that they use varieties other than used by their employer, to avoid conflict of interest situations. But the general permissiveness of winery owners in allowing their winemakers to have side projects is good for everyone, I think. It keeps the winemaker fulfilled professionally, it allows them to build their own brand gradually, and the dynamism created by new producers and new projects is good for the overall health of South African wine.

And, of course, this creates customers for old heritage vineyards, keeping them in the ground.

On a regional level, there is something to be said for legislation to protect significant vineyards. This is important where land has value for redevelopment. If it is zoned so that no one can build homes, but it has to be kept as agricultural land, then this is valuable. Urban spread is threatening many wine regions, and some legislation could help here. I was recently in the Hunter Valley, a brilliant historically significant Australian wine region. With its proximity to Sydney, this is quite a playground for city folk. If economics is left to decide the destiny of the land, then it’s likely that the vineyard area will further contract. You could end up with a wine region popular with tourists, but with hardly any vineyards.

But the best way to preserve important vineyards? Make them pay!

  • Jamie Goode is a London-based wine writer, lecturer, wine judge and book author. With a PhD in plant biology, he worked as a science editor, before starting wineanorak.com, one of the world’s most popular wine websites.

title: Editorial: Wine needs new consumers. Now what?
summary:
Over the weekend, a group of perhaps a dozen adults gathered around a braai. Two-thirds were English-speaking, one-third Afrikaans-speaking – an unusual enough combination to prompt a conversation about language. Why, someone asked, was I not fluent in Afrikaans despite having studied at Stellenbosch University? My response was that, at least, I had Afrikaans friends. […]

The post Editorial: Wine needs new consumers. Now what? appeared first on winemag.
content:
Over the weekend, a group of perhaps a dozen adults gathered around a braai. Two-thirds were English-speaking, one-third Afrikaans-speaking – an unusual enough combination to prompt a conversation about language. Why, someone asked, was I not fluent in Afrikaans despite having studied at Stellenbosch University? My response was that, at least, I had Afrikaans friends. What struck me afterwards was that I couldn’t say the same about having black friends.

The global wine industry faces a challenge that is now impossible to look past: consumers are drinking less.

There is less agreement about why. Demographic change, health concerns, economic pressure and competition from other alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages are all offered as explanations. The causes matter, but perhaps less than the consequence. Wine has a demand problem, and the old growth models are no longer available to solve it.

That ought to prompt a more radical question than how we tell wine’s story: What if the industry needs to change the way wine is experienced, discovered and discussed?

It dawned on me that a key part of the problem is not poor communication of a compelling consumer promise, but a lack of relevance at a more fundamental level. I wrote about this earlier this year, arguing that wine’s problem isn’t a shortage of stories but a shortage of reasons for people to care. That remains my view. The harder question is what needs to change.

Technology: opportunity or trivialisation?

The danger is that technology makes wine more accessible while making it more trivial. Wine has enthusiastically embraced digital marketing while remaining remarkably attached to analogue ways of helping people choose what to drink.

A consumer still encounters a shelf containing dozens of bottles, differentiated by labels, regions, varieties, vintages and producer names. The information required to make a confident choice can be considerable.

Technology can make this easier. AI, for example, could become a useful wine intermediary – not a robot sommelier making grandiose pronouncements, but a tool that translates expertise into the questions ordinary drinkers actually ask.

Is this dry? Full-bodied? Fresh and linear or soft and smooth-textured? What should I eat with it? Is there something similar but cheaper? If I liked this bottle, what else might I enjoy? Is this a wine to drink tonight or keep for five years?

These are not intellectually inferior questions. They are the questions that get wine into people’s glasses.

The opportunity, then, is not to use technology to produce more wine content. There is already plenty of that. It is to reduce the effort required to participate in wine. We don’t need an infinite number of tasting notes generated by machines – God forbid, humans are already adequate at that. We need better ways of connecting a particular person with a particular wine.

But there is a caution. Personalisation can easily become another form of narrowing, giving us more of what we already like while reducing the chance of encountering something unexpected. At the same time, digital wine culture has its own cliques, and the people within them can end up deciding what is fashionable, desirable or worth talking about. Technology may therefore democratise access to wine while creating new forms of gatekeeping around taste.

Its more interesting role would be to do the opposite: broaden discovery, expose people to wines and ideas beyond the circles they already inhabit, and make it easier for new voices to influence what wine becomes.

Who gets to define wine?

I am 55, white, male and based in Cape Town. I have spent more than two decades working professionally in wine. I know a great deal about the subject and have accumulated plenty of assumptions about what matters in wine, how it should be discussed and what constitutes expertise.

But the episode around the braai left me wondering how well equipped I am to understand what might make wine relevant to people whose lives and experiences have historically had so little meaningful contact with it. If my own social world can remain so racially circumscribed after 55 years in South Africa, perhaps the wine industry should be less surprised that its attempts to connect with black consumers so often feel superficial.

My experience has value. But it does not make me the ideal interlocutor with every future wine consumer. This is particularly pertinent when we talk about South Africa’s emerging Black middle class. The answer isn’t simply to market wine more effectively to Black consumers. Nor is it to recruit a handful of Black personalities as ambassadors while leaving the underlying culture untouched.

If new consumers are to become part of wine’s future, they need a genuine role in shaping it. That means more Black winemakers, yes, but also more Black retailers, sommeliers, marketers, educators, writers and entrepreneurs with the power to influence the category. It means allowing different social occasions, tastes and cultural references to shape how wine is presented and consumed.

And it means those of us who have traditionally occupied positions of authority accepting that relevance may involve giving up some control over the conversation. That isn’t a threat to expertise. It is a test of whether expertise can adapt.

The wine industry sometimes treats the new consumer as though they are waiting to be persuaded to appreciate what we already appreciate. That is the wrong starting point.

The more productive question is: what might wine become when people who have historically been outside its cultural centre start influencing it?

The answer should not be “wine dumbed down”. Nor should it be “wine as we know it, but with younger faces”. Nor should it be wine reinvented so completely that it loses any connection with its history.

The industry should retain the things that make wine worth caring about – place, craft, history, agriculture, diversity and pleasure – while becoming much less prescriptive about how consumers encounter them.

That may mean different formats, occasions, price points, voices and ways of talking about taste. It may mean wine appearing in spaces where it has not traditionally appeared, alongside food, music and culture without demanding that everyone first learn its vocabulary. One of the reasons I detest “minerality” as a descriptor is that it illustrates the problem perfectly: what insiders regard as useful shorthand can sound like nonsense to everyone else.

And it may mean accepting that some of the things enthusiasts consider important simply aren’t important to everyone else. That is not necessarily decline. It may be democratisation.

As we know all too well, vineyards are being pulled out and production is contracting. The difficult work now is not managing abundance but rebuilding demand. We cannot assume that the next generation will inherit wine culture simply because previous generations did. They have more choices, different media habits and different relationships with authority. They also have no obligation to preserve our hierarchies.

So what would I suggest? Use technology to make wine easier to discover and understand, without reducing it to disposable content. Communicate in ways that begin with consumers’ lives rather than wine’s internal vocabulary. Create more opportunities for participation rather than simply more opportunities to consume marketing. And, above all, broaden who gets to shape the category.

For someone like me, there is a final responsibility: to remain useful without assuming that I must remain central. That may be the hardest adjustment of all.

title: Recipe: Tofu, tat soi and shimeji mushroom stir-fry
summary:
Delicious served with steamed rice. Serves 4 Ingredients: 3 tbsp (45ml) sunflower oil 400g tofu, drained and patted dry with absorbent paper 60g shimeji mushrooms, cleaned ¼ cup (60ml) ginger, finely chopped 2 tsp (10ml) sesame seed oil 3 tbsp (45ml) soy sauce 3 tbsp (45ml) sweet chilli sauce squeeze of lemon 200g tat soi, […]

The post Recipe: Tofu, tat soi and shimeji mushroom stir-fry appeared first on winemag.
content:
Serve with Kruger Family Wines Old Vines Cinsault 2017.

Delicious served with steamed rice.

Serves 4

Ingredients:
3 tbsp (45ml) sunflower oil
400g tofu, drained and patted dry with absorbent paper
60g shimeji mushrooms, cleaned
¼ cup (60ml) ginger, finely chopped
2 tsp (10ml) sesame seed oil
3 tbsp (45ml) soy sauce
3 tbsp (45ml) sweet chilli sauce
squeeze of lemon
200g tat soi, washed
15g coriander, chopped
steamed basmati rice, to serve

Method:
Cube tofu into bite size portions and set aside.

Heat sunflower oil in a non-stick pan until hot and gently shallow-fry tofu until golden brown and crispy. Add mushrooms and ginger and stir-fry for further five  minutes. Add sesame oil, soy sauce, sweet chilli sauce and a squeeze of lemon.

Toss in tat soi and remove pan from heat allowing the leaves to wilt. Check seasoning.

Serve with steamed basmati rice and fresh coriander.

Wine pairing:
Light-bodied reds you can chill will work with this dish – think Pinot Noir or new-wave Cinsault.

  • Recipe supplied by Source Food – a Cape Town-based food agency that specializes in experiential marketing. They will create a recipe or meal to communicate your brand’s message.

title: Tim James: Growing older, drinking differently
summary:
We know about old vines and old wines – and their age makes a difference. But what about old wine-drinkers? Does age bring changes, for better or worse, in taste-experiences and preferences? It was a question that the American winewriter and -importer Terry Theise raised in the latest issue of World of Fine Wine, prompted […]

The post Tim James: Growing older, drinking differently appeared first on winemag.
content:
We know about old vines and old wines – and their age makes a difference. But what about old wine-drinkers? Does age bring changes, for better or worse, in taste-experiences and preferences? It was a question that the American winewriter and -importer Terry Theise raised in the latest issue of World of Fine Wine, prompted by his own experience (he didn’t announce it there, but tells me he’s 73). This led to wondering about physical changes that might prompt changes in taste: a supposed reduction in acuity, for example; and he mentioned the presumably hormonal changes in older women – but I guess those in men might also be expected to have consequences.

Theise was surprised, however, to find that most of the small handful of wine-professional friends and colleagues he consulted reported no significant patterns of change in their wine-tastes.

I too am surprised. Easy continuity is not my own experience, whatever the causes of my shifts. Given that I’ve noticeably changed my tastes in various aesthetic areas that are important to me, why not my wine-drinking? These days I seldom read novels, for example, and novel-reading was a defining factor of my life for decades, professional and personal. Overall I now read less than I used to, and it’s usually re-reading rather than anything new, and more often than not it’s non-fiction. My musical tastes have shifted too: it’s still all “classical”, but I can’t easily recall how much I used to love Italian opera (mostly unspeakably silly stuff, I now think, though often kitschly beautiful); and generally I have moved in both temporal directions away from the lushness of nineteenth-century Romanticism.

So, again, why not changes in my tastes in wine as I’ve got older? I’m now 71, having begun a more-or-less serious relationship with wine only in my latter 30s. I don’t think these changes are all obviously ascribable to bodily changes any more than are my shifts in musical and literary tastes … but, yes, maybe some. I have certainly had a general reduction in my taste for sweet foods and drinks in the last decade or two, and that is plausibly related to bodily changes. So my beloved older-style German rieslings often seem too sweet and I would reluctantly admit to, on the whole, preferring drier ones.

When acidity loses its appeal

This is something that Terry Theise strongly notices too. Interestingly (given the high acidity in the best of those sweet rieslings) he also notes a change that he says is more age-typical: a resistance to very high acidity in wines, a character he used to relish. I hadn’t thought of that for myself, but I think it applies. It would help explain why at tastings I seem to object more than my younger colleagues to the “hipster” style of lowish-alcohol, ultra-fresh wines, both white and red, and tend to find them unbalanced and even aggressive in their acidity.

Taking this further, I wonder if this also accounts for my mild turn in the last decade or so away from the red burgundies and local pinot noirs that I previously enjoyed so much more. I’ve returned more , in fact, to an earlier love: cabernet sauvignon-based blends – especially from Bordeaux, especially the dark-fruited, savoury, tannic and “sinister” ones that hark back to pre-1982 times (but seldom South African examples, which I can admire theoretically occasionally, but seldom love, because they are that bit too sunny and friendly, even when not too ripe and powerful). Tannin, then, suits me now more than acidity, it seems.

The pleasures of caring less

As to a decline in acuity – well, I don’t think I’ve ever been acute as a taster, nor have I aspired to become more so, though I realise that this might seem odd for someone who, for example, tasted and rated for the annual Platter’s Guide for two decades. Aiming for the finest, geekiest discrimination has never interested me nearly as much as other aspects of wine (social, historical, cultural, agricultural) – even less now. Decades back, I got through giving up smoking cigarettes without being aware that it made much difference to my palate. Having now joyfully abandoned writing more than the briefest of tasting notes has been an enormous liberation. (I can’t say I frequently read others’ notes either.) It’s very possible that this liberation has itself positively affected the way I enjoy wine in all circumstances: an aura of anxiousness – coming from a sense of responsibility and of my likely inadequacy – doesn’t cloud the pleasure.

There’s much less detail that I’m concerned with these days, Possibly that marks a decline. But I read, just this morning over my toast and marmalade, this apposite line from Montaigne about the comfort he finds in old age, in an essay entitled “All things have their season”:  “that it deadens in me many desires and cares by which life is troubled”, including “care for knowledge”. There’s so much about the vast world of wine that I no longer feel curious about, as I did when I would read the Oxford Companion to Wine cover to cover. That reduction in interest is more of an admission, I suppose, than a boast.

Some changes in my tastes – as reflected in my drinking practices – are clearly not so much so much about ageing as about my growing older in a particular place and time. I’ve had a good few decades chronicling – and drinking – the Cape wine revolution. South African fine white wine is, widely, a miraculously delicate, not to mention delicious, expression of its origins. In response, I now drink nearly as much white wine as red, and that’s a notable shift. As all wine gets more expensive, local and foreign, and I don’t get richer, it suits me well to buy and drink for my pleasure lots of Cape white, and little foreign white apart from sherry and what good German riesling I can afford.

As for the local reds, I prefer the Rhône-style ones, based on syrah or grenache – the whole range of them, including the lighter, fresher ones (but not too light) with no new oak. There’s another change, I think: I now get more pleasure than before from comparatively simple, fairly young wines. I don’t think I’d even want to drink only fine, mature, serious wines, even as an aspiration. Perhaps it’s a sign of greater tolerance.

Something else. I’ve always had a particular passion for fortified wine: sherry, port, madeira. But now, along with drinking some younger, lighter wines, I also go to the opposite extreme and drink a good amount of brandy. I seem to like that kick at the end of the day. My total alcohol consumption has probably declined a little in the last decade, but the proportion of the alcohol intake provided by brandy has increased.

That’s a change in my drinking habits that I am at a total loss to explain. The great revolutionary Leon Trotsky once said that “’Old age is the most unexpected of all things that can happen to a man.” That’s true, I think, and many of the details of the process are just as surprising.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.
